title: Road-type field codes motorways and dual carriageways separately only in 2013-2015, so the conventional and motorway figures describe the coding, not the roads
disclosure_where: Nothing on catalonia.html, Figure 1 or data.html Table 18. DATA_QUALITY_MICRODATA.md:373 gives pooled counts only. The only related remarks concern the cross-source harmonised model: data.html ('11 of 12 candidate variables ... (road type does not)'), validation.html ('Road type was left out because its coding disagrees on the crashes both sources hold'), methodology.md ('road class fails'), GENERALISABILITY.md:413, and ml_common_feature_validation.csv (road_class JSD 0.056). None says the Catalan field is coded differently by year, none qualifies the Catalonia page's road-type figures, and the validation page puts road-type coding breaks down to DGT's records.
factual_core: The Servei Català de Trànsit file's road-type field (D_TIPUS_VIA) codes motorways (Autopista) and dual carriageways (Autovia) almost only in 2013-2015. In 2010-2012 and 2016-2023, crashes on those roads are coded 'Carretera convencional'. The pooled 2010-2023 road-type figures on the Catalonia page therefore mix coding regimes and misdescribe roads: 1,981 of 3,093 fatal crashes on conventional roads, 18.8% of 10,540, and motorways at 20.5% from 'only 224 crashes' with an interval that overlaps conventional roads.
verifier_reproduction: Raw CSV (Any x D_TIPUS_VIA, pandas): Autopista by year 2010-2023 = 8,5,0,64,69,71,2,0,2,0,0,0,1,2, so 204 of 224 (91.1%) fall in 2013-2015. Autovia = 7,6,3,142,141,131,13,7,12,24,3,2,4,1 (414 of 496). The processed parquet is identical, so the break is in the source, not introduced by processing. AP-7 is coded Autopista 3,3,0,34,40,34,1,0,0,0,0,0,0,1 and conventional 44,32,52,0,0,0,30,30,40,32,23,30,55,45; A-2, C-32, B-23, T-11, A-7, C-17 and C-58 show the same pattern. DGT microdata for the same Catalan crashes with a death or serious injury within 24 h, 2016-2023 (12,957 crashes against the file's 12,961): toll plus free motorway 737 (180 fatal, 24.4%, 95% interval 21.5-27.6%); autovia 835 (178, 21.3%); conventional 4,650 (803 fatal = 49.4% of 1,627; 17.3%, 16.2-18.4%). For those years the file has 7 Autopista, 66 Autovia and 6,017 conventional crashes (1,113 fatal = 68.4%). Of the AP-7 crashes in 2016-2023, DGT codes 286 of 288 as motorway; the file codes 285 of its 287 as conventional. Reclassification of interurban conventional-coded crashes outside 2013-2015, three ways. (a) Per-road share of DGT's 2016-2024 interurban injury crashes coded 1-3: 2,240 expected high-capacity crashes (520 fatal); the 2016-2023 part is 1,583 (366 fatal), close to DGT's 1,572 (358). This gives conventional 8,300 crashes, 1,461 fatal (47.2% of 3,093), share 17.6% (16.8-18.4%); motorway 1,247 crashes, 22.4% (20.2-24.8%); dual carriageway 1,712 crashes, 21.5%. Hard rule (roads at least 90% high-capacity in DGT): 1,619 fatal (52.3%), 17.8%. (b) My own 2013-2015 5-km-section template: 1,913 crashes (436 fatal) moved; conventional 1,545 fatal (49.95%), 17.9% (17.1-18.7%); motorway 936, 25.0% (22.3-27.8%); strict rule 1,801 fatal (58.2%), 18.9% (18.1-19.7%). (c) Named autopistas AP-7, AP-2, C-32 and C-33 (interurban, any coding): 843 crashes (651 coded conventional, 190 Autopista), 210 fatal = 24.9% (22.1-27.9%). Leaving out the attacker's 16 roads: conventional 1,684/9,278 = 18.2%, 54.4% of fatal crashes. 2013-2015 under the file's own coding: conventional 341/673 fatal crashes (50.7%) at 16.8%; motorway 42/204 = 20.6% (15.6-26.7%). Every attacker number I checked reproduces.

(7) Road+km templates (v7) applied to conventional-coded interurban crashes. With the SCT 2013-15 template: 2010-12 ≈ 526 crashes (115 fatal) reclassified, 2016-23 ≈ 1,377 (321 fatal), total ≈ 1,903 (436 fatal); this reproduces the attacker's figure. The 2016-23 estimate agrees with DGT (aggregate gap 1,367 crashes / 310 fatal; linkage 1,497 / 341). The DGT template gives 600 crashes (132 fatal) for 2010-12. Measured codings only (SCT 2013-15 + DGT 2016-23): motorway 222/941 = 23.6% (21.0-26.4) vs conventional 1,144/6,680 = 17.1% (16.2-18.0), no overlap; conventional = 49.7% of 2,300 fatal crashes. (10) The study's own overlap check: road_class JSD 0.0563 > 0.005, validated=False (reports/tables/ml_common_feature_validation.csv; docs/GENERALISABILITY.md:347). (11) Calculator spillover (v10). Outside 2013-15, about 24% of the regional-owner conventional crashes (the calculator's reference) and about 40% of the State-owner ones lie on motorway or autovía sections (template estimate). severity_model.py _ROAD_TYPE maps D_TIPUS_VIA directly. The effect on the model's ratios was not quantified.
materiality: Fatal crashes on conventional roads would be about 1,460-1,620 of 3,093 (47-52%), or at most 1,801 (58%) under the strictest rule, instead of 1,981 (64%). 'Most' is therefore not established. The conventional fatal share would be about 17.6-17.9% (18.9% under the hard rule) instead of 18.8%, on about 8,300-8,600 crashes, not 10,540. Motorway crashes would number about 700-1,250 (3 to 5.6 times 224). Their fatal share would be 22.4-25.0%, with lower 95% bounds of 20.2-22.3%, above every reclassified conventional upper bound (18.4-19.7%), so the overlap clause reverses. DGT's own coding of the 2016-2023 crashes gives 24.4% against 17.3%. Dual carriageways would go from 496 crashes at 16.5% to about 1,700 at 19.5-21.5%, above conventional roads, which changes the ordering in Figure 1 and Table 18. 'Motorways had the highest share' survives. Spillover, not quantified: the calculator's State and regional (reference) conventional levels contain about 36% and 30% motorway and dual-carriageway crashes, and the model has no year term.
suggested_fix: Restrict the road-type shares to 2013-2015, the years the file codes motorways and autovias. Alternatively, reclassify from the road name (and km point): DGT's TIPO_VIA for 2016-2023 and a road or section template for 2010-2012. At minimum: state next to the paragraph, Figure 1 and Table 18 that the file codes motorways and dual carriageways separately only in 2013-2015; delete 'only 224 crashes' and the overlap clause; replace '1,981 of the 3,093' and 'most' with 'about half'; add a year-by-year road-type check to regional.py. Review the calculator's road levels for the same break.

title: Location contrasts (lead's 6.63, Table 1, 'urban crossing 8.75') are inflated by an outcome-dependent 'alignment unknown' level
disclosure_where: data.html, 'Missing values and regional recording' (repeated in docs/methodology.md §13 and docs/models/dgt_crash_severity.md). It says the level is 95.7% Catalan and 'describes recording practice'. It says 'A recording practice that goes with the outcome could distort the other coefficients through such a level' and refits without Catalonia, with 'All 32 other odds ratios stay inside the full model's interval' and the urban-crossing zone term moving from 4.28 to 2.57. Table 17 there shows the interurban zone moving 3.24→2.00 and the conventional road type 2.04→2.68. The model card says the level 'marks crashes recorded in Cataluña rather than a kind of road'. No document says that Catalan alignment is filled in almost only for severe crashes. The joint contrasts are never refitted. severity.html (the lead, Table 1 and the 8.75 sentence) has no caveat beyond a CSV link.
factual_core: In DGT's Catalan records, road alignment (TRAZADO_PLANTA) on non-street crashes is filled in almost only when someone died or was hospitalised within 24 h. Inside Catalonia, the model's 'alignment unknown' level (OR 0.12) therefore stands in for the outcome. The Catalan crashes whose alignment is recorded are selected for severity, and they feed the zone and road terms, so the joint location contrasts in the lead and Table 1 come out too high, the urban-crossing rows most of all.
verifier_reproduction: Recording pattern, from data/processed/dgt_accidentes.parquet. Catalan ZONA 1 crashes are 99.91% 'unknown' without a death or 24-h hospitalisation (n=65,313) and 24.57% with one (n=6,463). ZONA 2: 99.0% vs 57.1%. Rest of Spain: 1.41% vs 0.73%. Catalan non-street crashes: 94.75% unknown if not fatal, 21.25% if fatal. The 5,387 Catalan non-street crashes with alignment recorded are 97.3% serious and 22.5% fatal; the 75,624 unknown ones are 0.43% fatal. Street crashes carry only code 998, which is folded to 'straight'. 68.3% of urban-crossing crashes (9,153 of 13,407) are Catalan. Refits used the package's own features.model_frame, models.fit_severity and models.location_contrasts (CR1 by province), imported read-only. They reproduce Table 1 exactly: 6.63 (4.95–8.89), 8.75 (6.52–11.75), 7.23, 4.28. Leakage-free variants, giving interurban conventional / urban-crossing conventional / interurban motorway / urban-crossing urban street: - Alignment dropped: 5.69 (4.73–6.85) / 3.86 (2.68–5.56) / 4.72 / 1.92. - Unknown read as straight: 4.97 (4.17–5.92) / 3.76 / 4.41 / 1.82. - Catalan alignment alone set to the reference: 5.36 / 3.84 / 4.60 / 1.89. - Catalan non-street alignment all set to 'unknown' (a region marker carrying no outcome information): 6.23 / 5.64 / 5.87 / 2.73. - Without Catalonia: 5.36 (4.40–6.52) / 6.87 (5.35–8.81) / 4.77 / zone term 2.57. - Without Catalonia and without alignment: 5.40 / 6.83 / 4.77. - Province fixed effects without alignment: 5.05 (4.33–5.89) / 4.46 / 5.78 / 2.00. - Catalonia alone without alignment: 5.30 / 2.83 (2.59–3.09). Province fixed effects that keep alignment leave the inflation in place (6.77 / 8.23 / 9.27), as within-Catalonia leakage predicts. Urban-crossing conventional is the largest contrast only in the two no-Catalonia fits; in the other five it is below every interurban road type. Crash-type and junction terms barely move (alignment dropped: head-on 5.80, pedestrian 6.90, junction 0.689). Every number the attacker quotes was reproduced to within rounding.
second_check_numbers: Recording, from data/processed/dgt_accidentes.parquet with my own script (scripts/recording.py). "Serious within 24 h" means TOTAL_MU24H+TOTAL_HG24H>0. Catalan ZONA 1, not serious within 24 h: 99.905% alignment unknown (code 4), n=65,313. Serious within 24 h: 24.57%, n=6,463. Catalan ZONA 2: 99.0% (n=8,306) vs 57.1% (n=847). Rest of Spain ZONA 1: 1.41% vs 0.73%. All Catalan non-street crashes: 94.75% unknown if not fatal (n=79,472) vs 21.25% if fatal (n=1,539). By the 24 h outcome: 99.80% vs 28.4%. Catalan non-street crashes with alignment recorded (n=5,387): 97.3% serious within 24 h and 22.5% fatal. With alignment unknown (n=75,624): 2.7% and 0.43%. ZONA 3 (streets) is always 998 in both regions, so alignment carries no outcome information on streets. The project's own dgt_audit_outcome_recording.csv agrees: 0.212 vs 0.947. Refits of the fatal model, all with province-clustered 95% intervals: my own chunked IRLS and sandwich (scripts/myfit.py, scripts/extra_specs.py) on the study's own model frame (features.model_frame). The base fit reproduces Table 1 exactly: 8.75 (6.52-11.75), 7.47, 7.23, 6.75, 6.63 (4.95-8.89), 5.66, 4.28, 2.89, 1.74. Interurban/conventional and urban crossing/conventional under each leakage-free specification: - alignment dropped: 5.69 (4.73-6.85) and 3.86 (2.68-5.56) - Catalan alignment set to straight: 5.36 (4.54-6.33) and 3.84 (2.67-5.53) - unknown read as straight: 4.97 (4.17-5.92) and 3.76 - Catalan alignment ignored plus a Catalan non-street indicator: 6.23 (4.79-8.12) and 5.63 (4.48-7.08) - Catalonia indicator: 5.36 and 4.86 - province fixed effects without alignment: 5.05 (4.33-5.89) and 4.46 - province fixed effects with Catalan alignment ignored: 4.90 and 4.40 - province fixed effects plus the Catalan non-street indicator: 5.12 and 4.70 - without Catalonia: 5.36 (4.40-6.52) and 6.87 (5.35-8.81) - Catalan zone interactions: 5.42 and 6.78 Interurban motorway 7.23 falls to 4.40-6.04. The four interurban types fall from 5.66-7.23 to 4.72-5.69 with alignment dropped and 4.77-5.47 without Catalonia. Urban crossing/urban street 4.28 falls to 1.82-3.03, and urban crossing/other road 7.47 to 3.29-6.16. Head-on, pedestrian and junction with alignment dropped: 5.80, 6.90, 0.689. Within Catalonia alone, the published specification gives an interurban/conventional contrast of 48.4 and an urban crossing/conventional contrast of 37.4. Without alignment they are 5.30 and 2.83. 68.3% (9,153/13,407) of urban-crossing crashes are Catalan.
materiality: Conventional interurban: 6.63 becomes 4.97–6.23 across seven leakage-free specifications. The published value is 6–33% too high, but every alternative lies inside its interval and the direction holds. The four interurban road types go from 5.66–7.23 to roughly 4.4–5.8 (at most 6.2). Urban-crossing conventional goes from 8.75 to 3.76–6.87, so it is 27–133% too high; five of the seven estimates fall below the published lower bound of 6.52, and it is the largest contrast in only 2 of 7. Urban crossing/urban street goes from 4.28 to 1.82–2.73, urban crossing/other road from 7.47 to 3.30–4.86, and interurban motorway from 7.23 to 4.41–5.87.
suggested_fix: Refit the lead and Table 1 location contrasts with Catalan alignment neutralised, either set to the reference or with alignment dropped (for example with province fixed effects), and publish that version or the range. State on severity.html that Catalan alignment is recorded almost only for crashes with a death or a hospitalisation within 24 h. Remove the implied 'largest' ranking of the urban crossing and the site check 'a conventional road through a town has the largest location contrast'.

title: 'Did not last' exists only because the pre-trend is limited to bends; by the page's own QAIC rule, a 2004 level shift fits the pre-period better and two bends fit equally, and both give a lasting ~10% fall
disclosure_where: site/policy.html, right after the heading: 'The result depends on how the earlier trend is projected. A straight line gives ... a lasting fall, -9.5% on average ... That difference favours the bend without being decisive.' site/data.html adds 'it is still a selection step, which is why the alternative pre-trends ... are reported', and docs/methodology.md §14 says 'a preference, not decisive evidence'. Nowhere (pages, methodology, STATISTICAL_AUDIT, CLAIM_LEDGER) mentions level-shift or multi-change pre-trends, or other window starts. The Table 5 sentence 'every specification except the straight-line pre-trend' rests on 10 of 12 rows that share the Aug 2003 knot.
factual_core: Under the page's own pre-trend rule (QAIC on Jan 2000-Jun 2006 only, c = 1.6076, two parameters per searched change), an equally parsimonious level-shift pre-trend (Jan 2004) fits the pre-period better than the chosen Aug 2003 bend (QAIC 473.4 vs 476.2), and a two-bend trend ties (476.26). Both give a lasting 17-month fall (-11.5%, -9.5%) instead of the published transient -2.5%. So 'did not last' depends on allowing only continuous single bends.
verifier_reproduction: My own Poisson GLMs on the published monthly series. Anchor: the package code reproduces the published fit (step -7.08%, mean17 -2.48%, end +2.34%). Pre-period (78 months, 42 positions Jul 2001-Dec 2004), c = 1.6076: - Best level shift: Jan 2004, QAIC 473.38. Best bend: Aug 2003, QAIC 476.24 (difference 2.86). Straight line: 483.38. - The difference is 4.59 at c = 1.0, 3.00 at c = 1.53 and 2.47 at c = 1.86. - Four shift positions in 2004 beat the best bend. - Shift fit: -2.62%/yr with a -9.7% drop. Bend fit: -2.77%/yr, then -7.67%/yr. Main fit (HAC12), each pre-trend: - Shift Jan 2004: step -12.63% (-16.6, -8.5); mean17 -11.50% (HAC -14.9, -8.0; QP -16.0, -6.8); end -10.36%. - Two bends Nov 2003 + Nov 2004 (QAIC 476.26): step -10.91%; mean17 -9.45% (-14.2, -4.4). - Shift plus slope change at Jan 2004: mean17 -6.88% (-10.7, -2.9). - Straight line fitted from 2004 only: mean17 -5.99% (-8.2, -3.8). Model averaging: - One-change family (85 candidates): weight 0.649 on shifts and 0.350 on bends; step -10.36%; mean17 -7.92%. The Buckland interval is -15.2% to 0.0% with HAC errors (the attacker's -16.4% to +1.4% uses quasi-Poisson errors). - 2,779 one- and two-change candidates: the single-bend family gets 2% of the weight; mean17 -6.95% (-13.7, +0.4); 72% of the weight is on fits whose mean17 interval excludes 0. Window starts: - Extended one-change family, starts 1995-2002: mean17 from -9.0% to -12.5%, every interval excluding 0. - Bend-only family: the 1995 and 1997 starts give -9.0% and -9.2%, but 1993, 1998, 1999, 2001 and 2002 give -1.3% to -3.4%. - Allowing two knots sends 1995-97 back to Aug 2003 (about -3%) and moves 1998, 1999, 2001 and 2002 to -7.5% to -10.5%. Simulation (150 replicates): - Truth = shift plus a lasting -10%: the published procedure gives a mean of -4.7%, 'did not last' 38%, coverage 0.41 (attacker: -4.9%, 38%, 0.40). - Reverse (truth = the published bend, transient effect): the shift-allowing procedure picks a shift 49% of the time and reports a 'lasting' fall 62% of the time. Other checks: - The local slope over Jan 2004-Jun 2006 is -5.1%/yr (HAC -6.1 to -4.2), between the shift fit (-2.6) and the bend (-7.7). - Raw data: Aug-Dec 2003 was above 2002 in 4 of 5 months, and 2003 (5,399) exceeded 2002 (5,347). The drop starts in Jan 2004. - The 30-day/24-hour ratio shows no break in 2004 (1.149, then 1.142).
second_check_numbers: All computed with my own code (Poisson GLM, month dummies, linear time in months, HAC with 12 lags and no small-sample correction, as in policy.py), on monthly 30-day deaths parsed directly from data/raw/dgt/tables/series_historicas_2024.xlsx (sheet M_I-U_Meses). That series matches data/staging exactly and sums to 38,852 deaths over Jan 2000 to Nov 2007, as the page states. REPLICATION OF THE PUBLISHED FIGURES - Pre-period Jan 2000 to Jun 2006 (78 months), knots at the 42 positions Jul 2001 to Dec 2004, c = 1.607552 (Pearson dispersion of the best one-bend fit). - Bend at Aug 2003: QAIC 476.239. Straight line: 483.383 (difference 7.14). This reproduces published Table 3 exactly. - Full window, bend at Aug 2003: step −7.1% (−13.2 to −0.5), 17-month mean −2.5% (−7.8 to +3.2), end of window +2.3%, back on the projection at month 12.2 (July 2007). - Straight line: −12.0%, −9.5% (−14.3 to −4.5). - Bend fixed at Jan 2004: −7.0%, −2.1%. - All match Table 5. LEVEL-SHIFT FAMILY (same 42 positions, 15 parameters, same as a bend) - Best is Jan 2004: QAIC 473.38, 2.86 better than the best bend. Pre-period fit: slope −2.6%/yr, drop −9.7%. - Bend minus shift as c varies: +4.59 at c = 1.0, +2.86 at 1.6076, +2.47 at 1.86, +1.53 at 3.0. - Full fit: step −12.6% (−16.6 to −8.5); 17-month mean −11.5% (HAC −14.9 to −8.0; quasi-Poisson −16.0 to −6.8); end of window −10.4%. - Next best shifts: Jul 2004 at 473.66 (mean −10.1%) and Jun 2004 (mean −10.3%). TWO BENDS - Best pair at least 12 months apart, Nov 2003 + Nov 2004: QAIC 476.28 against 476.24, a tie. Step −10.9% (−15.9 to −5.6); mean −9.5% (HAC −14.2 to −4.4; quasi −18.4 to +0.5); end −8.0%. - Best pair with no spacing limit, Dec 2003 + Jan 2004 (the same as a level drop plus a slope change at Jan 2004): QAIC 474.70, or 472.70 if counted with 16 parameters, the best fit of all. Step −9.6%; mean −6.9% (HAC −10.7 to −2.9; quasi −14.2 to +1.1); end −4.1%. Not back on the projection by Nov 2007; it would be at about month 27. QAIC-WEIGHTED AVERAGE - Over straight + 42 bends + 42 shifts: weight 0.649 on shifts and 0.35 on bends. Step −10.4%; mean −7.9%. - Burnham–Anderson variance with quasi-Poisson errors: −16.4 to +1.4, the attacker's figure. - Buckland 1997 with HAC errors: −15.2 to 0.0. - 70% of the weight is on pre-trends whose own 17-month interval excludes zero. - Adding level-plus-slope (broken) trends: mean −7.0% (HAC −14.1 to +0.7). - Bends and straight line only: −3.2% (−8.9 to +2.8). WINDOW STARTS (same rule, each January) - Bend-only family: - 1994 to 1997 starts pick knots in 2000 and give a lasting fall: −9.0%, −9.0% (−13.6 to −4.1), −9.5%, −9.2% (−14.0 to −4.2). - 1993 and 1998 to 2002 starts pick 2003 knots: −3.4% to −1.3%. - With level shifts added: every start from 1995 to 2002 gives a 17-month mean of −9.0% to −12.5%, and every quasi-Poisson interval excludes zero. - The 2000 start (policy.py:73) is not justified in methodology §14. ARTEFACT CHECK - The yearly 30-day/24-hour ratio barely moves: 1.149 in 2003, 1.142 in 2004. - On 24-hour deaths, which the police counted directly, the best shift (Jul 2004) still beats the best bend: QAIC 466.58 against 467.60. It gives −11.0% against −2.9%. LOCAL SLOPES (quasi-Poisson, month terms) - 2000 to 2003: −2.3%/yr. - Jan 2004 to Jun 2006: −5.1%/yr (−7.7 to −2.5). - This lies between the level-shift projection (−2.6%) and the bend projection (−7.7%). SIMULATION (my own code, 300 replicates each, negative binomial noise matched to dispersion 1.89) - Truth = Jan 2004 level shift plus a lasting −10%. The published rule picks a bend 64% of the time. Median step −6.9%; mean 17-month estimate −5.0%; interval coverage 41%; ends above the projection ("did not last") 28%. The attacker reported −7.1%, −4.9%, 40% and 38%. - Reverse, truth = the published bend fit. The rule with level shifts added picks a shift 50% of the time. Mean estimate −4.6% against a true −2.5%; interval excludes zero 60%. - A margin of at least 2.86 for the shift occurs 86% of the time under the shift truth and 17% under the bend truth, a likelihood ratio of about 5.
materiality: Only single continuous bends (and the quadratic) support these statements: the heading 'An immediate fall of about 7% that did not last', 'rejoin the projected path in about July 2007', 'the earlier months favour a trend that bends once', and the summary's single figure -2.5% (-7.8% to +3.2%). title: The 'comparable 2014–2023, +49%' for interurban illegal manoeuvres depends on a threshold 2% above the series' own 2017 jump
disclosure_where: factors.html, next to the claim: 'rose on interurban roads from 25.4% to 37.8%, a level they had already reached by 2017', which signals the step. Under Table 1: the rule 'cannot say whether a break, or a trend within a run, comes from behaviour, from recording or from both'. Technical notes (data.html): 'The threshold is a convention, and every change is published with its test so that another threshold can be applied ... the rule rules out only single-year jumps'. The 1.2234 ratio is in the factor_changes.csv download. Nowhere does the study say that this run sits about 2% under the threshold or would split at 20%. Table 1 still labels it 'Comparable years 2014-2023'. SECOND_AUDIT.md:29 shows the point was raised before and left as the 'by 2017' phrase.
factual_core: From 2016 to 2017 the interurban illegal-manoeuvres share rose x1.2234 (31.9% to 39.0%). Table 1 shows one comparable run, 2014-2023 (+49%), only because BREAK_RATIO = 1.25 is above that ratio. At any threshold of 1.2234 or less (for example 1.20) the series breaks in 2017: 2014-2016 is +26% and 2017-2023 is -3%.
verifier_reproduction: Year-to-year ratios recomputed from reports/tables/factor_shares.csv. I checked the counts against the PDF's Tabla 11 with pdftotext (6,495; 7,060; 8,211; 10,353; ...; 9,463), and factor_changes.csv line 76 holds the ratio 1.223413288 with is_break False. Interurban manoeuvres ratios: 1.1344 (2015), 1.1084 (2016), 1.2234 (2017), then 0.909-1.050. I ran the package's own factors.comparable_windows read-only. The defaults reproduce factor_windows.csv exactly. At break_ratio 1.20 or 1.2234 the run splits into 2014-2016 (25.4% to 31.9%, +25.7%) and 2017-2023 (39.0% to 37.8%, -3.2%). For any ratio from 1.2235 to 1.5744, every zone-level non-drug run is identical to the published one. The 2017 log ratio of 0.202 is the largest of the 69 non-break zone-level non-drug year-to-year changes (empirical SD 0.081). The next largest, urban distraction 2015 at 0.198, lies inside a 2-year run that Table 1 does not show. Interurban distraction also jumped x1.150 in 2017. The sum of the four interurban non-drug shares was 0.743, 0.772, 0.825 and 0.926 in 2014-2017, then 0.86-0.91. A logit that rises to 2017 and is flat afterwards has Pearson dispersion 15.6, against 139.5 for a linear trend over the decade. Yearbook Table 6.1.I, my own parse: STOP + other priority + overtaking + following distance = 8,601, 8,824, 9,387, 10,543, 10,593, 10,681 (2014-2019). That is +22.6% to 2017, against +59.4% for the crash-level factor count, so the attacker's numbers are right. But the unknown share in the driver-infraction block jumped from 13% in 2015 to 37% in 2016. Per known driver the rise is larger, and scope, unit and definition all differ, so this corroboration is weak.
materiality: Under a 20% rule, Table 1's row 'Illegal manoeuvres, Interurban, 2014-2023, 25.4% to 37.8%, +49%' becomes two rows: 2014-2016 +26% and 2017-2023 -3%, and the level is flat after 2017. The share-scale log-linear trend over 2014-2023 is +33% (95% +4% to +69%) and fits a step poorly. The facts in the text (25.4%, 37.8%, the level reached by 2017) stay true. What fails is the 'comparable' label and reading +49% as a change over the decade. No other Table 1 row, and nothing in the lead, changes at 1.20. The summary never mentions manoeuvres, so 'headline' slightly overstates the row's prominence.
suggested_fix: Beside Table 1, or in the manoeuvres sentence, add: 'the 2017 rise of 22% is just under the 25% break rule; at a 20% rule the series breaks in 2017 and is flat from 2017 to 2023 (-3%)'. Alternatively, show the run as 2014-2016 and 2017-2023.

title: On urban streets the heavy-vehicle excess is confined to crashes with pedestrians and two-wheelers; the model's additive flags spread it to car-versus-lorry crashes
disclosure_where: Not disclosed. SEVERITY_CALCULATOR.md:378-380 mentions the model's 'additive structure' only for rare combinations with fewer than 20 similar crashes, and the urban car+heavy side collision has 36. The same report (line 347) states 'on the urban reference crash x2.55 (2.08–3.12)' without a caveat, and sev_contrasts.csv:86 gives the same figure. The calculator shows 9.4% (7.2–12.0%) with no warning.
factual_core: On urban streets, the heavy-vehicle association depends strongly on whether a vulnerable road user (pedestrian, cyclist, moped or motorcycle) is involved, so the published model's additive user flags are rejected there. As a result, the model's urban car-versus-lorry contrast (x2.55; 9.4% vs 3.7%) is not supported by urban crashes between motor vehicles. Adding the term barely moves the interurban headline but cuts the urban reference contrast to about 1.7.
verifier_reproduction: Raw urban sub-zone (12,272 crashes): - No vulnerable user: heavy 8.2% (21/257) vs 9.8% (121/1,239), ratio 0.84. - With a vulnerable user: 19.8% (135/683) vs 5.6% (567/10,093), ratio 3.52. Published design (by_zone, provinces) plus an urban heavy x vulnerable-user column: - Unpenalised likelihood-ratio statistic 17.52 on 1 df, p = 2.8e-5 (sklearn and statsmodels agree). - Urban heavy-vehicle odds ratio: 1.29 (0.74–2.22) without a vulnerable user, 3.69 (2.62–5.21) with one. - The term is significant in each period: LR 6.10 (p = 0.013) in 2010–2016 and 10.16 (p = 0.0014) in 2017–2023. Interurban term: LR 4.72 (p = 0.03). - Raw Mantel-Haenszel, urban two-unit car+heavy vs car+car by crash type: 6.5% (n=93) vs 7.2% (n=387), risk ratio 0.96, odds ratio 0.96 (0.39–2.36). At the published C=0.1 (my refit reproduces the exported coefficients to within 5e-9): - Urban reference contrast falls from 2.55 to 1.68 (bootstrap 1.33–2.19, 200 resamples). - Interurban reference: 1.97 (1.73–2.25); 1.89 if an interurban term is added too. Out of sample: - Rolling 2016–2023 test with C fixed: log loss improves by 0.00045 per crash (SE 0.00014), and by 0.00079 (SE 0.00026) on urban crashes. - Project's own 2022–23 validation: 0.33207 → 0.33187. Calculator scenarios: - Urban side collision car+lorry: published 9.35% (7.24–12.00%) vs 6.3% with the term. - Pedestrian struck by a lorry: 18.3% vs 20.5%. Motorcycle+lorry: 13.6% vs 15.6%.
materiality: Headline unaffected: the interurban reference stays at 1.97 (1.89 with both zone terms), so 'about twice' on index.html holds. The published calculator and the linked report overstate the urban car-versus-lorry association: - x2.55 (2.08–3.12) becomes x1.68 (1.33–2.19); - the estimate of 9.4% becomes about 6.3%, which lies outside the calculator's printed interval. Urban crashes involving a vulnerable user and a heavy vehicle are slightly underestimated (pedestrian 18.3% vs 20.5%). A statistician would call this a failed additivity assumption that biases some of a published tool's outputs, not an error in the headline.
suggested_fix: Add a heavy x vulnerable-user term (at least on urban streets) to the calculator model; it improves the nested log loss. Alternatively, state on the model page and in SEVERITY_CALCULATOR.md:347 that on urban streets the excess with lorries and buses comes from crashes with pedestrians, cyclists and motorcyclists, and withdraw the urban x2.55 for crashes between cars and lorries.

title: Newey–West(12) intervals undercover even when the model is right; with valid errors the step and the slope change are not significant
disclosure_where: policy.html lead ('The model's intervals are too narrow: at 6 of the 14 other Julys...'), Figure 2 caption, and the placebo paragraph (calibrated -21% to +3%). data.html model paragraph ('Even so, the July placebos show these model-based intervals to be too narrow'), placebo paragraph ('The other intervals ... probably too narrow as well') and Table 5 caption. Not disclosed anywhere: that the estimator is biased under a correct model, that the residuals are serially uncorrelated (data.html gives month-to-month correlation as the reason for using Newey-West), and what the intervals would be with valid errors.
factual_core: Every interval in the case study uses Newey-West errors with 12 lags and no small-sample correction (policy.py:197, 301). For the main fit (95 months, 16 parameters), the residuals show no serial correlation. The NW12 standard errors are smaller than both the HC0 and the quasi-Poisson ones, and the NW12 intervals undercover badly even when the model is right. With valid model-based errors, neither the step nor the slope change excludes zero.
verifier_reproduction: v01_refit.py, which uses the package's own segmented_fit and choose_trend_knot, reproduces q8_points_sensitivity exactly: step -7.08% (-13.20,-0.52), slope +7.51%/yr (+1.35,+14.04), mean -2.48% (-7.83,+3.17). A hand-coded sandwich equals statsmodels HAC12: se(post) 0.03478, se(post_t) 0.002506. HC0: 0.0443 and 0.00494. Quasi-Poisson (phi 1.886): 0.0422 and 0.00382. Plain Poisson, which ignores overdispersion: 0.0307 and 0.00278. So NW12 is below even plain Poisson for the slope. Pearson residuals: lag-1 autocorrelation -0.10 (white-noise band +/-0.20). Ljung-Box p = 0.33, 0.67, 0.94, 0.74, 0.83 at lags 1, 3, 6, 12, 24. Durbin-Watson 2.11. Raw deaths have lag-1 correlation 0.73, but that is trend and season. Intervals with valid errors: quasi-Poisson step (-14.45,+0.92), slope (-1.73,+17.61)/yr, mean (-9.05,+4.56). NB2-ML (alpha 0.00134): step -6.99% (-13.56,+0.07), slope (-1.03,+16.03). HC0: step (-14.81,+1.36), slope (-4.29,+20.77). NW12 with n/(n-k): step (-13.77,+0.13). NW6: (-13.69,+0.04). Own coverage simulation (v02_coverage.py: own IRLS and sandwich, fitted bend model as truth, independent NB2 noise, 2000 replicates). With alpha matched to Pearson phi 1.886, NW12 covers the step 68.4%, the slope 63.9% and the 17-month mean 72.3%; quasi-Poisson covers 95.6%, 96.1% and 94.8%. With the ML alpha: NW12 68.2/64.3/73.8%, quasi 95.0/95.2/95.2%. Two nuances. (1) In this sample the realised NW12 step SE is at the 97th percentile of its null distribution (median 0.021; v02b). The published intervals are therefore 18% (step), 34% (slope) and 19% (mean) narrower than quasi-Poisson ones, not half as wide. The 73% figure describes the procedure, not this particular interval. (2) NW3, NW18, NW24 and plain Poisson also exclude zero for the step, but all of them are biased here, so 'only under this estimator' is slightly loose.
materiality: Step: -13%..-1% becomes -14%..+1% (quasi-Poisson) or -14%..0% (NB2-ML), so it no longer excludes zero. Slope change: +1.4%..+14.0%/yr becomes -1.7%..+17.6%/yr, so it no longer excludes zero, which removes the statistical support for the 'did not last' reading. 17-month average: -7.8%..+3.2% becomes -9.1%..+4.6%, with the conclusion unchanged. All 12 rows of Table 5, the 'Negative binomial' row included, widen by roughly 10-50%. The page's conclusions ('cannot show that the licence caused the fall, or that it lasted') stand and are strengthened.
suggested_fix: Compute every interval with quasi-Poisson (Pearson-scaled) or NB2-ML model-based errors, or with HC0 scaled by n/(n-k). Replace 'are correlated from month to month' with the residual diagnostics (Ljung-Box p >= 0.33), or drop it.

Street vs interurban odds ratios in that model: - Head-on: 2.79 (2.26–3.44) vs 5.60 (5.00–6.27). - Run-off: 5.06 (3.16–8.12) vs 1.50 (1.26–1.79). - Object/animal: 3.37 vs 0.70. - Pedestrian: 5.87 (4.96–6.95) vs 7.27 (5.74–9.22). Head-on crashes involve 2 vehicles in 89% of cases in both settings, so their gap (about 2.8 vs about 5.4) is real. Crude fatal shares on streets are reproduced: side 0.29%, head-on 0.91%, pedestrian 1.73%, run-off 1.70%. 70% of fatal crashes (10,093 of 14,333) and 93% of fatal head-on crashes are interurban, so the pooled odds ratios mainly describe interurban roads.

The head-on odds ratio there is about 2.8, half the lead's 5.48, and run-off and object strikes are as strong or stronger (typical-crash run-off 5.8 against pedestrian 6.3). title: Calculator's '95% confidence interval' is conditional on one model choice and a shrunken estimator, so it under-covers
disclosure_where: Calculator page notes: 'Its 95% interval covers only the uncertainty in the model's coefficients, not the differences between places and years' (tool_calculator.py:261). Severity-models Table 1 caption: 'The intervals cover the uncertainty of the model's coefficients only.' The rare_level warning: 'its interval does not show how few records there are'. The calculator report, linked from the page notes, says explicitly that the intervals do not reflect 'the uncertainty of the choices of penalty, specification, through-town rule and province intercepts' (docs/research/SEVERITY_CALCULATOR.md:389-391). The attacker missed this. Undercoverage from shrinkage bias is disclosed nowhere.
factual_core: The calculator's interval expit(x'b ± 1.96 sqrt(x'Vx)) uses a bootstrap covariance of the L2-penalised by_zone, C=0.1 coefficients. It ignores two things. First, the choice of specification and penalty: the choice was not decisive, and the runner-up specification moves estimates materially. Second, shrinkage bias: even when the model is true, its coverage of the model's own share falls below 95%.
verifier_reproduction: I refitted with the repository's own sm.records()/sm.fit_logistic, read-only. Max |refit − exported coef| = 5e-9. sev_choices confirms the published validation losses: by_zone 0.332066 vs common 0.333415, both at C=0.1. The nested selection chose common in 2017 and 2018, with C from 0.01 to 1000. Common C=0.1 fit against the published interval: - Outside for 25.3% of the 21,458 non-through-town training crashes (median |diff| 1.44 pp, p90 4.81 pp). - Outside for 19.8% of the 12,120 unique profiles. - Outside for 32.8% of 7,927 unique unwarned form scenarios drawn uniformly from the form (median 4.9 pp, p90 14.6 pp). - Default crash: published 13.41% (11.05–16.18%) against 10.89% under common. Other penalties within by_zone: C=0.0316 and C=0.316 put 0.0% of training profiles outside. C=0.01 puts 13.0% outside, and common at C=1000 puts 25.5% outside. Specification choice on 2022–23 validation (by_zone − common): −0.00135 log loss per crash, which is −3.9 nats over 2,910 crashes. Paired-bootstrap 95% CI −0.0050 to +0.0023; by_zone better in 76% of resamples. Sandwich SEs match the published 500-draw bootstrap SEs (median ratio 1.00, 5–95% range 0.94–1.06). Simulation design: parametric, 300 replicates on the 22,638-crash design, refitting by_zone at C=0.1. Results with truth = published coefficients: - 93.7% coverage on 3,000 sampled non-through-town training crashes. A check on 10 replicates × 100-draw bootstrap gave 93.5%, against 93.5% for the sandwich on the same replicates. - 97.7% for the default crash. - 90.0% on unwarned uniform form scenarios, with 14.5% of them below 80%. - 93.0% on warned scenarios. - Mean SE / true SD = 1.00, and coverage using the true SD is the same. The shortfall is therefore shrinkage bias (median |bias|/SD = 0.21). Results with truth = a C=1 fit: 92.0% on training profiles, 85.3% on unwarned form scenarios, 90.8% on warned ones. Table 1 ratio intervals on the severity-models page cover 91–96% when truth = published. With truth = C=1, coverage falls to 0.787 for 'urban street' and 0.847 for '40–50 km/h'. The expected out-of-sample calibration slope of a C=0.1 fit is 0.99, 1.01 and 1.01 under the three truths. The published slope of 1.03 therefore cannot exclude the less-shrunk truths. A penalised-Hessian (Bayesian) SE would be a median 6.6% wider than the published SE (p10–p90: 0.4–14%).
materiality: For profiles like recorded crashes, a nominal 95% interval covers the model's own share about 92–94% of the time, a shortfall of 1–3 points; the default/reference crash is covered. For unusual combinations shown without warnings, coverage is about 85–90%, with roughly a sixth of them below 80%. Where specification uncertainty applies it is material: the runner-up specification moves a quarter of recorded profiles outside the interval (median 1.4 pp, p90 4.8 pp), and the reference crash from 13.4% to 10.9%. No published conclusion is reversed. The '95%' label is moderately anti-conservative, and it is conditional on the selected model, which the page only implies.
suggested_fix: On the calculator and model pages, say that the interval is conditional on the chosen specification and penalty. Then either widen it (penalised-Hessian/Bayesian covariance, or a bootstrap that repeats the whole selection) or state that it can under-cover for unusual combinations of inputs.

title: The 95% range behind "outside its range" leaves out the chance that the trend changes, and at 4-5 years ahead it is badly miscalibrated
disclosure_where: long-run.html, in the sentence before the claim, defines the range as 'where a year would be expected to fall had the trend's last segment gone on with its ordinary scatter'. The summary says 'an excess that depends on where the trend starts'. After Table 1 the page gives the 2013 start (10%/8%, at the edge / within) and says 'the two readings differ because the trend kept falling after 2019'. data.html (long-run-projections) says 'the trend asks whether the decline of 2011-2019 went on'. Nowhere does the study say that the range leaves out the trend changing course, which this series did in 2002 and 2011, or how such ranges did out of sample.
factual_core: The 'outside its range' verdict for deaths per tonne of fuel in 2023 and 2024 uses a 95% prediction interval around the 2011-2019 refit. The interval covers delta-method trend uncertainty and quasi-Poisson scatter with t(7), and it assumes the slope carries on. Applied to origins before 2020, the same method's ranges miss most years four to five years ahead. A smooth-trend model that lets the slope change puts both years inside.
verifier_reproduction: I wrote my own IRLS (common.py). It matches statsmodels and longrun_series.csv exactly: 2023 ratio 1.1616 against an upper bound of 1.1060, 2024 1.1434 against 1.1120. A log-scale interval also leaves both years outside (upper 1.112 and 1.119). Raw CORES fuel and DGT deaths match the panel (v7). Rolling backtest (v2): origins 2003-2014, search on 1996..T, refit of the last segment, projection of T+1..T+5. Misses by horizon were 1/12, 3/12, 5/12, 7/12 and 7/12. Horizons 4-5 pooled: 14/24, the same with 24-hour deaths. Segments of 8 years or more: 8/8 outside. All match the issue. The 14 misses come from only two slope changes seen through overlapping windows: origin 2003, after the decline sped up around 2002-03 (2 misses), and origins 2008-2013, after it slowed around 2011-13 (12 misses). Smooth-trend UC model, 1996-2019 (v3): 2023 1.200 (0.749-1.334) and 2024 1.192 (0.687-1.455), both inside. Its own backtest still misses 4/24 at horizons 4-5, and its intervals are ±30-45% wide. The attacker's own runs that disagree were left out of the evidence. The UC random walk with drift on 1996-2019 gives 2023 1.387 against 1.253 (outside), and on 2002-2019 1.413 against 1.285 (outside). OLS on the log rate 2011-2019 gives 1.160 against 1.109 and 1.141 against 1.116 (both outside). Start sweep (v1) reproduced: start 2012, 2024 at 1.122 against 1.125 (inside); start 2013, 1.103 against 1.105 and 1.076 against 1.114. 10 of 11 alternative search settings keep 2011 as the last turning point (v6). Bootstrap (v4, B=2000) asks how often the range holds a fresh 2023/2024 value when the trend does carry on, with the turning-point search re-run in every replicate. Coverage was 93.8%/94.2% with dispersion 2.80 and 97.0%/96.7% with dispersion 1.55. The range is calibrated for what the page defines it to be.
materiality: The point excesses (+16%, +14%) do not change. 'Outside its range' and '(above)' stay literally true under the page's conditional definition, and the range covers about 94-97% when that condition holds. If the range also allowed for the trend changing course, as the smooth-trend model does, both years would read as within (upper bounds 1.334 and 1.455), and the heading's contrast with the count would weaken. Other structural or OLS forms keep them outside. The fix is a sentence of context, not a retraction.
suggested_fix: After 'outside its range' on long-run.html, add: 'The range assumes the 2011-2019 decline went on; it does not allow for the trend changing course, as it did in 2002 and 2011, and ranges built this way missed most pre-2020 years four to five years ahead.' Alternatively, call 2023-2024 'above the continued 2011-2019 trend' and give the smooth-trend interval beside it.

title: Admissions verdicts are knife-edge: the scatter window, one dropped year or a multiplicity correction flips them
disclosure_where: The trends.html summary and section 2 call the count 'at the edge' and say the per-tonne excess would vanish with 0.3%/yr more km per tonne. data.html and methodology section 4 give the dispersion factors' chi-square intervals and the t5 widening. No page reports window, leave-one-year-out or multiplicity sensitivity.
factual_core: Under the published construction, admissions per tonne have t = 2.96 on 5 df (p = 0.031, lower bound +1.6%), and the count has p = 0.052 (lower bound -0.2%). This is the only 'beyond' among 13 rows. The verdicts flip with the scatter window, with dropping one year of 2013-2019, with the quantile, or under a multiplicity correction.
verifier_reproduction: v4_knife.py uses risk_annual_panel.csv (which matches the raw yearbook) and risk_index.csv (bounds reproduced to 1e-9). Per fuel: t 2.961, p 0.0315. Count: t 2.533, p 0.0523. Holm over 13 rows gives 0.409 and Bonferroni x5 gives 0.157. With the normal quantile, the count's lower bound is +2.4% and per fuel +4.2%. Windows: 2014-19 per fuel -0.5%, 2015-19 -1.8%, 2012-19 count +1.0%. Leave-one-year-out: dropping 2013/2015/2018 gives -0.5/-0.2/-0.4%; dropping 2014/2016/2017/2019 gives +1.1/+2.0/+2.0/+1.3%. Of 24 windows of 5-12 years ending 2017-2019, per fuel is beyond in 7 and the count in 2; of the 6 starting in 2013 or later, 3 are beyond. All reproduced. In the study's defence: 15 of the 24 windows start before 2012 and straddle admissions' steep fall (dispersion 13.5-167), so they are not equally defensible. The repository's own joinpoint_search, applied to admissions, puts the last turning point at 2011 (count) and 2010 (per fuel). The 2011-19 window gives per fuel +0.9% and 2012-19 gives +2.8%. With the per-fuel rate's own dispersion (fuel as offset), the excess is beyond for every start year 2010-2013 (lower bounds +1.4%, +2.5%, +3.2%, +3.9%). CLAIM_LEDGER.md confirms the count was 'beyond' before the switch to Student's t.
materiality: The per-tonne verdict is borderline. Across reasonable constructions its lower bound runs from about -1.8% to +3.9%, and after Holm over 13 rows it is not significant, so 'beyond it' in the summary should say just beyond or borderline. The alternatives most tied to admissions' own trend strengthen it rather than reverse it, so 'about half of equally defensible constructions reverse them' is overstated.
suggested_fix: Call the per-tonne excess borderline (lower bound +1.6%, p about 0.03 under the page's construction). Add one sentence on its sensitivity to the scatter window and to dropping a year, and do not single it out in the summary without that qualifier.

With 40 deaths against a baseline of 375 over three Aprils, the 95% interval of the per-tonne ratio includes 1, and the size of the fall depends on the baseline and on applying the early-year adjustment only to petrol and toll.

April 2020 had 40 deaths; the 2017-19 Aprils had 141, 119 and 115 (mean 125). Ratios against that baseline: deaths 0.320, road fuel 0.4228, petrol 0.2364, diesel 0.4629, toll 0.2223; per tonne 0.757 (-24.3%). Per-tonne 95% interval: Clopper-Pearson 0.532-1.050, mid-p 0.540-1.039, Wald with phi=1 0.546-1.049 (p=0.094), with the page's dispersion 1.356 0.518-1.106 (p=0.15). Deaths change with phi=1.356: -78.1% to -53.2%. Deaths against petrol: 1.354, p=0.069 (phi=1) and 0.118 (phi=1.356). Against toll: 1.439, p=0.029 and 0.060. On the page's own early-year reckoning (petrol Jan-Feb 1.145, toll 1.094): against petrol 1.55, p=0.024; against toll 1.575, p=0.019 (phi=1.356). Baselines: 2019 -14.9%, 2018-19 -17.6%, 2017-19 -24.3%, 2016-19 -25.8%, 2015-19 -25.4%, 2014-19 -27.9%. Jan-Feb 2020 against 2017-19: deaths 0.957 (257 vs 268.7, z about -0.6, so noise), fuel 1.043 (1.024 per day, since February 2020 had a leap day). Adjusting both deaths and fuel gives -17.5%; fuel only -21.1% (-22.5% per day). Ordinary Aprils against the mean of the three preceding usable years: per-tonne SD 0.172 (n=9); 2015 -17.2%, 2019 -16.6%, 2024 -15.1%, 2023 +34.8%. Code: seasonality.py:183-217 computes point ratios only; site/seasons.py:277-287 prints them; :144-147 checks only that the change is below 0. LOCKDOWN_BASELINE has been (2017, 2018, 2019) since 7897aeb, so I found no sign the baseline was chosen to suit the result.
materiality: No published number is wrong: -68%, -58%, -76%, -78% and -24% all reproduce. With a 95% interval of about -47% to +5% (exact) or -48% to +11% (the page's dispersion), the -24% per-tonne change cannot be told from no change (p 0.09-0.15). suggested_fix: Add an interval and a qualifier to the paragraph, for example: 'so deaths per tonne of road fuel fell 24% (95% interval: a fall of 48% to a rise of 11%), within the variation of an ordinary April; against a 2019-only or a 2014-2019 baseline the fall is 15% or 28%.' Soften the fuel half of the heading, for example 'deaths fell about as much as traffic: by more than road fuel sold, a difference within chance, and less than petrol or motorway traffic'. Replace the sign-only guard at seasons.py:144-147 with one on the interval.

title: The per-tonne month pattern depends on how freight is weighted: 'February below' and 'August above' do not survive light-vehicle denominators
disclosure_where: The claims are labelled 'per tonne of fuel'. The lead adds 'but other measures of traffic disagree about August', and the section 2 heading 'The measures of traffic disagree about August, so the excess per kilometre is unknown' is next to the claim, but for August only. That fuel mixes freight with private travel is in methodology lines 369-370 and in trends.html#road-fuel, linked from section 2. Figure 2 shows the petrol and toll indices by month (February: deaths 84, fuel 91, petrol 85, toll 83), but the text never says February also depends on the measure. By singling out August, the page implies the rest of the pattern does not.
factual_core: Road fuel weights heavy vehicles above their share of kilometres, and heavy traffic has its own seasonality. As a result, the per-tonne month pattern depends on the freight weighting. With petrol, or with fuel net of a freight component, the intervals for February (and March under petrol) and for August include 1. July and September above, and April and May below, hold under every measure. The page warns about August only.
verifier_reproduction: I wrote my own quasi-Poisson GLM, the same model as seasonality.month_effects. It matches the published road-fuel effects to 5e-10. Per tonne of petrol: Feb 0.989 (0.926-1.055), Mar 0.953 (0.895-1.014), Apr 0.914 (0.858-0.974), May 0.926 (0.870-0.985), Jul 1.061 (1.004-1.121), Aug 0.978 (0.924-1.035), Sep 1.065 (1.005-1.129). Per tonne of diesel the pattern matches road fuel (Feb 0.909, Aug 1.118). Per tonne of 'light fuel' (road fuel minus a share s with the seasonality of heavy toll vehicle-days): at s=0.2, Feb 0.933 (0.874-0.996) and Aug 1.047 (0.989-1.108); at s=0.3, Feb 0.940 (0.880-1.003), Mar 0.929 (0.872-0.990), Aug 1.019 (0.963-1.079), Jul 1.102 and Sep 1.086, both above; at s=0.4, Feb 0.948 (0.887-1.014). Per toll vehicle-day, February is above (1.085, 1.018-1.157) and July and August below (0.922, 0.790). Heavy share of toll traffic by month: Feb 0.168, Aug 0.083. August index: heavy vehicle-days 88.4 against light 150.9; diesel 101.9 against petrol 116.1. Table 1.2.14 gives an interurban heavy share of 10.6-11.8%; the 4-5x fuel per km is an assumption. Motorcyclists are 18.1% of February deaths and 27.1% of July deaths (microdata, 2016-19 and 2022-24).
materiality: Every published per-tonne number and interval is correct. Read as risk per unit of traffic, which the lead invites by calling fuel 'the only monthly measure of traffic on all roads', February is as measure-dependent as August: below per fuel and diesel, null per petrol and per light fuel at s of 0.3 or more, above per toll. March is null per petrol. The robust part is April and May below, and July and September above. The heading 'February to May below it' holds per tonne, but February's reading per unit of traffic needs the same caveat August already has.
suggested_fix: After the August caveat, add: 'They disagree about February too: per tonne of petrol February is 0.99 times the average month (0.93-1.06) and per toll vehicle it is above it. April and May lie below, and July and September above, under fuel and petrol alike.' Optionally publish the per-petrol month effects beside the per-tonne ones.

title: Outcome-dependent recording cannot be bounded; modest differentials would produce every interurban ratio
disclosure_where: speed.html, section 'The ratio describes police records, not measured speeds', directly below Table 1: 'Police may look harder for speed when someone has died, which would raise it ... The data cannot measure either bias.' The same page's lede says the ratios are 'associations in police records, not estimates of what speed causes'. The home page intro says each comparison is 'an association in the records, not an estimate of what caused it'. Methodology section 9 ends with the two biases; factors.py docstring. The size of the differential that would produce each ratio is not given anywhere.
factual_core: Suppose speed has no real effect, there are no false positives and deaths are rare. If police record speed k times as often in fatal crashes, the deaths-per-crash ratio comes out at about k. So the interurban ratios (1.22, 1.75, 1.90) need only a modest k, while the urban 5.90 needs about 5 to 6. Nothing in the repository can bound k.
verifier_reproduction: Recomputed the ratios from the staged speed report (Tables 13-15, 2016-2023) against in-scope microdata totals. Deaths: 5.895 urban, 1.896 motorway, 1.222 dual carriageway, 1.753 other interurban (equal to speed_severity_pooled.csv). Hospitalised injuries per crash: 2.494, 1.373, 1.271, 1.457. Non-hospitalised: 1.067, 0.942, 0.947, 0.924. Exact algebra under the null with rare deaths: R = k(1-q)/(1-kq), where q is the recorded share (3.2%, 11.4%, 14.0%, 19.1%). The k needed is then 5.10 urban, 1.72 motorway, 1.19 dual, 1.53 other interurban, slightly below the attacker's k ~ R, so the point holds more strongly. Driver tables 6.1 (staging tables_driver_infractions, all Spain): unknown speed status 40.0-49.1% of interurban drivers and 51.8-62.4% of urban drivers in 2016-2024, against 17-20% in 2014-15. Barcelona 2025 raw files: 31 of 6,851 injury crashes have the mediate cause 'Excés de velocitat o inadequada' (0.45%, 1 death), against 11,085/346,004 = 3.2% of urban crashes in the report's scope. This compares two different recording schemes, so it is only illustrative. Neither the report nor the microdata has a crash-level speed measurement, an agency field or speed by time of death.
materiality: No published number changes. Every sentence is about crashes 'in which the police recorded' speed and stays true. As evidence about speed, the interurban ratios are fragile: they would be fully produced if fatal crashes had speed recorded about 1.2-1.7 times as often as non-fatal ones. The urban ratio would need roughly five-fold differential recording. Its hospitalised-injury ratio (2.49) also points the same way, so the 'most of all on urban streets' ranking is robust.
suggested_fix: Add one sentence to the speed page's recording paragraph. With no real difference, recording speed k times as often after a death gives a ratio of about k. The interurban ratios (1.2-1.9) are within reach of such a differential; the urban 5.9 would need it about five-fold.

title: The 2.00 (1.69–2.36) summary depends on the pooling frame; random-effects intervals are far wider
disclosure_where: speed.html, next to the claim: 2.00 is called 'their weighted summary' after the 1.22-5.90 range, and the paragraph after Table 1 says it 'describes no single kind of road: it is weighted towards other interurban roads'. The data.html technical notes and methodology.md section 9 give LR 446 on 3 df, the fall in dispersion from 13.5 to 2.0, and 'a weighted summary, dominated by other interurban roads'. Not stated: that the interval holds only for that fixed weighting and would be several times wider for a typical road type. The home page gives 2.0 with the 1.2-5.9 range and no interval.
factual_core: The 2.00 (1.69-2.36) summary is the speed coefficient of a common-ratio quasi-Poisson model: 64 cells, 52 df, dispersion 13.48, z quantile. The data reject a common ratio (LR 446 on 3 df). Other standard summaries give 1.92-2.22. Random-effects intervals over the four road types are several times wider (DL 1.09-4.51, HKSJ 0.75-6.56, prediction interval 0.07-71). So the stated precision applies only to a fixed-set, death-weighted reading.
verifier_reproduction: v_pooled.py: quasi-Poisson 2.0000 (1.6922-2.3638), scale 13.476, df 52; t(52) gives 1.686-2.373, which is immaterial. LR 446.40 on 3 df. Of the Pearson X2 of 700.8, 602.1 lies in the 3-df speed x road-type interaction; the 49-df remainder is 98.6 (phi 2.01). Across road types with Poisson variances: fixed effect 2.1654 (2.071-2.264), Q 531.6, I2 0.994. With year-overdispersed variances: fixed effect 2.0995 (1.967-2.241), Q 230.8. DL 2.2148 (1.0889-4.5053); REML 2.2152 (1.1322-4.3341); Paule-Mandel 2.2152 (1.1344-4.3259); HKSJ t(3) 0.7474-6.5637; prediction interval t(2) 0.069-71.2. Random-effects weights are about 0.25 each; fixed-effect weights are 0.65 on other interurban roads. Mantel-Haenszel over 32 strata 1.9663 (1.8812-2.0553); road x year stratified quasi-Poisson 2.0053 (1.6240-2.4761); O/E 1.9207; direct standardisation to the all-crash mix 2.7486. A year-block bootstrap of the published estimator (2,000 replicates) gives 1.80-2.20. A grep of site/*.html, the page extracts and methodology.md finds no use of 'random effects' for this summary; the 'brief' the attacker cites is its own brief, not published text.
materiality: No published number changes. Under the reading the page states (a weighted summary of four road types that partition all crashes), the published interval is conservative: fixed-set intervals are narrower (fixed effect 1.97-2.24; year bootstrap 1.80-2.20; published 1.69-2.36). Only under a random-effects 'typical road type' reading, which the page disclaims, is it 4.2 times (DL) to 6.5 times (HKSJ) too narrow in log width. The point value is robust at about 2 (1.92-2.22). What remains is wording: 'its interval is widened to allow for how much the ratios differ', and the home page's 2.0 without the weighting named.
suggested_fix: Replace 'its interval is widened to allow for how much the ratios differ' (and the Figure 1 caption's 'also for the differences between road types') with a statement of scope: e.g. 'its interval applies to this weighting of the four road types; it is not a range for any one road type, whose ratios run from 1.22 to 5.90'. Optionally note in the technical notes that an unweighted (random-effects) mean over the four types is about 2.2 with an interval of about 1.1-4.5.
